sections.heading: C — Fitness, vision, fatigue and impairment
sections.markdown:
## C — Fitness, vision, fatigue and impairment

FACT_ID: sec13-F01 | anchor: A01
The staged manual describes a pre-license vision test requiring at least 20/40 vision in one or both eyes, with corrective lenses allowed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F02 | anchor: A01
Peripheral vision helps detect vehicles and hazards beside you while looking ahead; use mirrors and side glances as needed too. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F03 | anchor: A01
Clear eyesight alone does not ensure accurate judgments of distance or speed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F04 | anchor: A01
Distance and speed judgment matter when choosing merge or passing gaps and assessing a train before crossing tracks. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F05 | anchor: A01
If night vision or headlight glare is troublesome, the manual advises limiting nighttime driving to necessity and taking extra care. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F06 | anchor: A01
Wear the glasses or contact lenses you need for driving whenever you drive. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F07 | anchor: A01
Avoid dark glasses and tinted contacts at night because they reduce the light available for vision. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F08 | anchor: A01
Fatigue can impair seeing, alertness, decision speed and decision quality. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F09 | anchor: A01
Tiredness may increase irritability and can lead to falling asleep at the wheel. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F10 | anchor: A01
Get your usual night’s sleep before a long trip and plan departure for a time when rested. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F11 | anchor: A01
The fatigue guidance flags medicine that causes drowsiness as a trip risk. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F12 | anchor: A01
The handbook advises a light pre-trip meal because a large meal can make some people sleepy. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F13 | anchor: A01
On a long trip, the source recommends rest stops about hourly or whenever needed and allowing ample time for the trip. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F14 | anchor: A01
Its rest-break examples include walking, fresh air and coffee, soda or juice; these are presented alongside its separate prohibition on driving sleepy. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F15 | anchor: A01
Do not drive while sleepy; stop to sleep rather than relying on the hope of staying awake. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F16 | anchor: A01
Where possible, another driver can take over while you sleep. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec13-F17 | anchor: A02
Alcohol can impair judgment as well as driving skill, including the ability to recognize when to stop drinking. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F18 | anchor: A02
Alcohol slows reactions and reflexes, impairs clarity of vision and reduces alertness. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F19 | anchor: A02
Increasing alcohol levels worsen judgment, distance and speed estimates, and control of the vehicle. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F20 | anchor: A02
Even a single alcoholic drink can affect driving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F21 | anchor: A02
The manual’s comparison defines one drink as 1½ ounces of 80-proof liquor, 12 ounces of beer, or five ounces of wine. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F22 | anchor: A02
A specialty drink may contain alcohol equivalent to several ordinary drinks. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F23 | anchor: A02
The source says coffee, fresh air, exercise and cold showers do not sober someone quickly; it identifies elapsed time as the factor. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F24 | anchor: A02
When attending an event with alcohol, arrange a designated driver, transit or an available cab. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F25 | anchor: A02
Prescription and nonprescription medicines can impair driving, sometimes with effects comparable to or worse than alcohol. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F26 | anchor: A02
Medicines for headaches, colds, allergies or calming nerves may cause drowsiness and affect driving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F27 | anchor: A02
The manual warns that stimulant or diet pills may briefly increase perceived alertness but later cause nervousness, dizziness, poor concentration or vision effects. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec13-F28 | anchor: A03
Check medicine labels for driving warnings; ask a doctor or pharmacist about side effects if unsure whether driving is safe. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec13-F29 | anchor: A03
The handbook warns against combining alcohol with other drugs because their effects may multiply or add and can seriously harm health and driving ability. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec13-F30 | anchor: A03
The source identifies illegal drugs, including marijuana in its example, as a driving-impairment concern. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec13-F31 | anchor: A03
Illness or discomfort, including a cold, stiff neck, cough or sore leg, may impair driving; let someone else drive when unwell and needing transportation. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-nm-l:new-mexico-motor-vehicle-division-taxati:handbook:pdf-0033]

Misconceptions: feeling alert or drinking coffee does not establish sobriety or fitness to drive; a legal BAC figure does not define an unimpaired amount.
Mnemonics: rested, seeing clearly, sober, and attentive before driving.
Glossary: BAC is blood alcohol content; peripheral vision detects activity beside the forward view; fatigue reduces alertness.
Dynamic facts: current medical licensing standards, medication effects, impairment law and local phone restrictions require review.

verification_debt.claim_text: The20/40 requirement, night-vision advice, medication/fatigue guidance and physiological claims are from an edition-unconfirmed manual. Current issuer and clinical review is required; no medicine-stopping instruction, caffeine remedy or individual medical clearance is supplied.

Page33 places marijuana in an illegal-drug discussion. The indexed statement describes that old source context and a driving-impairment concern, not present possession/use legality or a modern scientific study result. Current official/legal and clinical review is required.

Page31 gives an undated about40% fatal-crash involvement statistic. Page32 says alcohol reaches the brain in20–40minutes, the body removes one drink/hour, and two or more drinks in the bloodstream mean impairment/arrest risk. These broad, time- and person-dependent source claims are withheld from indexed driving rules pending current official/clinical review; they are not a waiting-time calculator, safe amount or assurance about arrest.
